planet.plain_summary: This looks like a planet about 1.5 times the size of Jupiter that circles its star every 3.1 days.
key_facts: Estimated from how much starlight is blocked and the star's size.
Earth-size < 1.25, super-Earth < 2, Neptune-size < 6, Jupiter-size < 25 Earth radii.
Time for one trip around the star.
1 AU is the distance from the Earth to the Sun.
Rough temperature if the planet reflects 30% of the starlight and spreads the heat evenly. Degrees Celsius = kelvin minus 273.
How much of the star's light is blocked during each dip.

variable.plain_summary: Not a planet, but still interesting: this star changes brightness on its own; it gently pulsates, brightening and fading every 2 hours.
key_facts: Hot stars a bit heavier than the Sun that pulsate in small, regular ways.
Time for one full cycle of brightening and fading.
How much the brightness varies (5th to 95th percentile).
How much of the brightness change one regular cycle explains. Near 1: very regular (pulsation); low: irregular (spots that come and go).
How much the period differs from one observing sector to the next.

Strength of the second harmonic relative to the first: 0 for a smooth wave, larger for sharp, lopsided cycles such as pulsating stars. Values above 1 usually mean the period found is a multiple of the true one, so they are not shown.
Gaia classifies it as: Delta Scuti / Gamma Doradus pulsator
Cached Gaia variability classification (stars brighter than Gaia G = 11).
